name: Counting Functions (Total / One-One / Onto / Bijective / Boolean)
recognitionClueHinglish: 'How many functions', 'number of one-to-one functions', 'number of onto functions' — seedha counting poocha gaya hai between two finite sets. Sabse bada cluster hai is topic ka (14/30 PYQs).
whatShouldComeToMind: First check: |domain|=m, |codomain|=n — and whether m<n, m=n, or m>n, since that decides WHICH formulas are even possible.
Total functions = n^m. One-one needs m≤n = P(n,m). Onto needs m≥n = inclusion-exclusion sum. Bijective needs m=n = n!.
If reverse-given (told the COUNT, asked for |A| or |B|) — set up the formula as an equation and solve.
generalSolvingApproach: 2. Match the question's keyword (any function / one-one / onto / bijective) to the corresponding formula.
3. For onto counting via inclusion-exclusion: Σ_{k=0}^{n} (-1)^k C(n,k)(n-k)^m — compute term by term, don't skip the alternating signs.
4. For reverse-direction questions, set formula = given count, solve for the unknown.
variationsObserved: Codomain is itself a power set (functions INTO 2^B) — combine with power-set-size formula from Set Theory.
Probability variant: randomly pick a function from all n^m, find probability it's one-one = P(n,m)/n^m.
Constrained counting: bijections with a fixed point condition (f(x)≠x for some x, or f(1)=k) — adjust via direct casework on the constrained elements first.
commonTraps: Using n^m formula when the question actually asks for ONE-ONE or ONTO specifically.
Forgetting m≤n is required for one-one to be possible at all (else answer is 0).

name: Injective/Surjective/Bijective Verification & Composition Reasoning
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek specific function di hai (formula se, jaise f(x)=x² ya piecewise) aur poocha hai one-one/onto hai ya nahi, ya f aur g compose karke banaye gaye g∘f ke baare me poocha hai — ye property-verification/composition pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: For equal-size FINITE sets: one-one ⟺ onto ⟺ bijective — check just ONE of them if |A|=|B|.
For composition g∘f: g∘f onto ⟹ g is onto (not necessarily f). g∘f one-one ⟹ f is one-one (not necessarily g). Memorize this direction — it's asymmetric and a favorite trap.
For infinite sets (like ℝ→ℝ or ℕ→ℕ), the equal-size shortcut does NOT apply — must check both properties independently.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. If domain and codomain are both finite and same size, just check ONE property (say, injectivity) and conclude bijective if it holds.
2. Otherwise, check injectivity directly: assume f(a)=f(b), derive whether a=b is forced.
3. Check surjectivity directly: for arbitrary y in codomain, can you always find x in domain with f(x)=y?
4. For composition questions, use the two memorized composition rules above rather than re-deriving from scratch each time.
variationsObserved: Descriptive/older-style explicit proof required (1988, 2001 papers) vs modern MCQ-style TRUE/FALSE.
Inverse function computation for an explicit bijective formula.
commonTraps: Applying the equal-finite-size shortcut to infinite sets.
Getting the composition-implication direction backward (assuming g∘f onto implies BOTH f and g onto — false, only g is guaranteed).

name: Image/Preimage of Sets Under a Function (f(A∩B) vs f(A)∩f(B) style identities)
recognitionClueHinglish: Question me f(A) ya f⁻¹(B) jaisi notation hai, aur A/B ke union/intersection ke saath combine karke ek identity TRUE hai ya nahi poocha hai — ye ek narrow but recurring GATE trap-pattern hai.
whatShouldComeToMind: Preimage (f⁻¹) is 'well-behaved': distributes over BOTH ∪ and ∩ perfectly, always.
Forward image (f) is 'partially behaved': distributes over ∪ always, but only gives ⊆ (not =) over ∩ — equality needs f injective.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify whether the identity involves forward image f(·) or preimage f⁻¹(·).
2. If preimage: both ∪ and ∩ identities are TRUE, always.
3. If forward image with ∩: it's generally FALSE as an equality (only ⊆ holds) unless the question also states f is injective.
4. If forward image with ∪: it's TRUE as an equality, always.
commonTraps: Assuming image behaves identically to preimage — it doesn't, intersection is the asymmetric case.

name: Equivalence-Classes-via-Function (kernel/quotient) & Advanced Combinatorial Counting
recognitionClueHinglish: Function se induced equivalence relation (a~b iff f(a)=f(b)) define hoti hai, ya function ki jagah matrices/subsets ka function-jaisa counting hota hai — ye advanced/hybrid pattern hai, mostly recent (2021+) tough questions.
whatShouldComeToMind: Every function f:A→B induces an equivalence relation on A: a~b iff f(a)=f(b). The equivalence classes are exactly the 'fibers' (preimages of single points).
If f is onto, the number of equivalence classes = |B|.
'Bijection between matrices/subsets and functions' framing — recognize the underlying set is secretly a function space in disguise.
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Identify the 'disguised' function space (e.g., an m×n boolean matrix ≡ a function from {1..m}×{1..n} to {0,1}).
2. Translate the question into standard function-counting/property language.
3. Apply the relevant counting or property pattern from above.
commonTraps: Not recognizing the disguised function-space framing and trying to solve from scratch.

name: Misc Concrete Function Puzzles (encoding schemes, functional-equation recursion, boolean identities)
recognitionClueHinglish: Ek specific, self-contained function-based puzzle hai jo upar ke patterns me clean fit nahi hota — jaise ek prime-based encoding scheme, ya ek recursive functional equation (f(2n)=..., f(2n+1)=...), ya ek boolean-algebra identity check. Low-frequency but worth recognizing as 'read carefully, work from the given definition directly' rather than forcing a memorized formula.
whatShouldComeToMind: No single formula applies — read the custom definition very carefully and work forward from small concrete cases.
conceptsRequired: Careful reading + basic number theory/boolean algebra as needed per question
generalSolvingApproach: 1. Work out the function's behavior on the first few small inputs by hand.
2. Look for a pattern before attempting the general case.
commonTraps: Trying to force-fit a memorized counting formula onto a custom-defined function.
